prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling frequency measurements at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: B008 has the broadest support in the opening ballots (six of eight members ranked it, five in their top three, two first places) and, more importantly, it holds up on the experimental evidence. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the Stark shift that limits trapped-atom clocks while letting many atoms be interrogated at once, and Ye's group converted that into record systematic uncertainty and stability, with the many-body and spin-exchange understanding that explains why the clock works at that level. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by several independent laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg), and international comparisons are routine, which is the reproducibility standard I care about. The consequences are concrete rather than rhetorical: millimetre-to-centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy, tighter limits on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings, and the clock technology behind the planned redefinition of the second. Two names give a clean allocation of the invention and its leading realisation, and the group is not forced to draw an arbitrary line through a thousand-person collaboration.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier time-and-frequency prizes (Hall and Hansch 2005 for the comb, Wineland and Haroche 2012 for single-quantum-system control), which some will see as having already honoured this lineage. There is also a real attribution risk, because lattice clocks were built in parallel at SYRTE, PTB, NIST and elsewhere, and the invention can be argued as Katori's alone with Ye's contribution being performance and physics rather than concept. Finally, the SI second has not yet been redefined, so one could argue the story is unfinished. I do not think any of these is decisive, but the committee should state clearly in the citation that the prize is for the lattice-clock invention and its realisation at 10^-18, not for clocks in general.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B008 first and says the two credited names carry the central contributions, noting that she can judge the atomic-structure and systematic-shift calculations directly, and that earlier clock prizes laid groundwork without covering this invention.
responses.response: I agree on the pair and on the non-overlap with 2005 and 2012. I would add a qualification from the laboratory side: the 10^-18 claims rest on a handful of systematics (blackbody radiation shift, lattice hyperpolarisability, density shifts) that were controlled differently in the JILA and RIKEN/Tokyo systems, and the fact that independent systems now agree in comparisons is what makes the claim solid, not any single uncertainty budget. Your question about waiting for the SI redefinition I would answer with no: the prize is for a measurement capability that already exists and is already used, and delaying would tie a physics prize to a metrology-committee timetable.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first on the grounds that it opened microwave quantum optics on a chip and underlies essentially all superconducting qubit readout and gates, and he flags both possible overlap with the 2025 prize and his own proximity to the community.
responses.response: I ranked B012 third and take the architecture argument seriously, since the strong-coupling measurement was clean and reproducible. My difficulty is the combination of the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which makes a return to the same platform this soon hard to justify when other fields are waiting, and the attribution gap: Girvin and Huang wrote the 2004 proposal with Blais and Schoelkopf, and no three-name set repairs that. I would keep B012 as a serious alternative, but I do not see it displacing B008 unless the committee decides the 2025 prize left the cQED architecture unrecognised. I note your own ballot also ranks B008 second, so we may be closer than the first-place columns suggest.

responses.point: Olsson ranks spherical-aberration correction (B009) first as a clear instrument invention that opened atom-by-atom imaging, and asks whether it is physics or a methods contribution suited to another prize field; she also flags her own proximity to microscopy.
responses.response: I sympathise, since I put great weight on instruments that let us observe what could not be observed before, and the corrected TEM clearly qualifies on impact and maturity. But the same measurement-first logic favours B008 on the physics: the lattice clock does not just improve an existing capability, it makes new observables available (gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, constants searches) that bear directly on fundamental physics, whereas the corrector's principal outputs are in materials characterisation. Your own attribution caveat about Krivanek and the STEM-side correctors is also a real obstacle to a clean three-name credit, and the discipline question you raise would remain open at the prize stage. I would keep B009 as a candidate for a later year rather than this one.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first, as a landmark of instrument-driven astroparticle physics that opened neutrino astronomy, and treats Halzen and Karle as a natural compact pair with some allocation questions about AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers.
responses.response: I accept that a new messenger is exactly the kind of observational opening I value, and the diffuse-flux result is robust. My hesitation is the evidentiary maturity of the astrophysical story you also flag: the individual source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are at moderate significance and most of the flux is still unattributed, so the discovery that is secure is the existence of the flux, not what produces it. By contrast B008 is secure both in performance and in independent reproduction. I would rank B042 below B008 for now but would not object to it as a future candidate once source identification matures.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize as already covering the lattice-clock invention, or as complementary groundwork.
Whether the citation should foreground Katori's invention and Ye's realisation separately, and whether competing lattice-clock groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST) change the attribution beyond these two names.

Whether a combined two-achievement prize (for example B008 with a condensed-matter or particle-physics part) would be preferable to a single measurement-technology prize, given the three-person cap that makes a split awkward.
Timing relative to the pending SI redefinition of the second.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Jun Ye is closely associated with Hall's JILA group, so there is a possible personal connection to B008 that the committee may wish to consider for recusal; I have no direct collaboration with either credited laureate. I am also in the leadership of WACQT, whose superconducting-qubit work relies on circuit QED (B012), and WACQT overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, Johansson's home institution.
